The applicant, Mr Anthony Boner, is a British citizen born in 1960. He lives in Glasgow, Scotland. The applicant, through his solicitor, lodged an intimation of intention to appeal against conviction. An application to extend legal aid to the appeal proceedings had been submitted in May 1990. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr Ulf Jacobson, a juris candidate practising in Stockholm. The patient had incurred extra costs for medical treatment, foot rails, soft shoes, home assistance, and to some extent his food budget because of a limited ability to prepare meals. He also had to pay for the transportation service for disabled persons, and extra travel by personal car, because of his considerably reduced ability to walk. On 16 July 1997 the Social Insurance Office (försäkringskassan) of the County of Stockholm rejected the application. The applicant appealed against the lower court's judgment to the Stockholm Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) requesting it to quash the judgment and refer the case back for fresh examination. By a judgment of 13 February 1998 the County Administrative Court rejected the applicant's appeal on the grounds that the medical and other evidence in the case showed that, even before he had reached the age of 65, he had for a considerable time been functionally impaired. The applicant was entitled to disability benefits at a level corresponding to 36 % of the basic amount as of July 1994. He further requested that the court hold an oral hearing, on the same grounds as those he had presented to the lower court. He submitted that, by refusing to hold a hearing, the latter had breached Article 6 of the Convention. The Supreme Administrative Court (Regeringsrätten) rejected the applicant's request for a hearing and refused him leave to appeal.

It lays down various legal means designed to counteract and/or redress the undue length of judicial proceedings. A party to pending proceedings may ask for the acceleration of those proceedings and/ or just satisfaction for their unreasonable length under section 2 read in conjunction with section 5(1) of the 2004 Act. The Supreme Court ruled that while the 2004 Law produced legal effects as from the date of entry into force, its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date.

The applicant was born in 1943 and lives in Wrexham. She was in receipt of long-term incapacity benefit. At age 60, which is the date of entitlement to the State pension for women, she ceased to be eligible for IB. In its place she became entitled to draw her state retirement pension which, based upon her contribution record, entitled her to GBP 57.81 per week (about 62% of the maximum rate) She continued to draw DLA. As a result, the applicant claimed that she was some GBP 24.04 per week worse off as a result of her transition from IB to State pension. The applicant complained to the Department of Work and Pensions concerning the differential treatment but was informed that nothing could be done.

The prisoner appealed the decision, and the appeal was dismissed. The case was dismissed on the grounds that it was not a case of the patient being denied access to his own medical letter, but of the matter being referred to as a matter of law by the court. The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life. On 7 February 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of theApplication at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant was concerned that his attempts to confirm that he was receiving adequate treatment in hospital might be regarded by the prison medical officer as criticism. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence with his external medical specialist being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor subsequently reconsidered his decision after seeking advice from HM Prison Service Headquarters. On 20 February 2004 the presiding High Court judge, Mr Justice Collins, allowed the applicant's claim for judicial review. The Court of Appeal concluded that although the procedure set out in the prison governor’s letter of 28 November 2002 amounted to an interference with the applicant's right to respect for his correspondence, the interference was justified and proportionate. Lord Justice Sedley gave the judgment of the court. It was noted that there was no dispute that the reading of prisoners’ correspondence was governed by law, and that it was directed to the prevention of crime and the protection of the rights and freedoms of others. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse, for example, if the applicant's prison life or treatment was made more difficult because of what he was observed to be writing. Petition for leave to appeal was refused by the House of Lords on the ground that the petition did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. The applicants did not comply and, by letter of 2 April 2004, the company gave the applicants notice of termination of the tenancy agreement with effect from 31 July 2004. The Board noted that the fact that the new satellite installation extended through a window did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. With regard to the general obligation to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house, the Board considered that the actual installation did not and could not damage the house.

The Board found that the fact that the new satellite installation extended through a window did not involve a breach of Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants dismantled the satellite dish and installed a new device by placing on the kitchen floor an iron stand from which an arm was mounted. The Rent Review Board gave a decision on 21 October 2004 finding in their favour. The landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal (Svea hovrätt). The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr Tornefelt gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision of 20 December 2005, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations. The court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. It concluded, contrary to the findings of the Rent Review Board, that its placement breached Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. Although their satellite installation did not pose any real safety threat, their interests could not be allowed to override the weighty and reasonable interest of the landlord that order and good custom be upheld.

Bryan Stanford was convicted of indecent assault, rape, kidnapping and making a threat to kill. He is serving a ten-year sentence in Her Majesty’s Prison Long Lartin, in Worcestershire. The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in France. His wife died on 26 March 2001. They had no children from the marriage. His claim for widows’ benefits under the new system in place as from 9 April 2001 was made on 4 May 2001 and was rejected on 4 June 2001. On 10 July 2001 the applicant appealed. In a decision of 23 July 1996 the court noted that the issue in the case was whether the applicant's extra costs attained the level required for a disability allowance under the 1962 Act. The court ordered the National Social Insurance Board (Riksförsäkringsverket; hereinafter ‘the Board’) to submit observations in the Case. The Board answered by a letter of 13 August.

The Board appealed against the judgment to the Administrative Court of Appeal and submitted a medical certificate from a further physician, who stated that an increased consumption of fluids was necessary due to the applicant’s handicap but that there was no particular need for mineral water. The applicant reiterated his request for an oral hearing on 22 May 1997. He now stated that he wished to be heard in person about his working conditions and the costs of his Consumption of fluids. The court rejected this request, saying that it was unnecessary and rejects the request to that effect. The Board then appealed against this decision and the Court gave judgment in favour of the Board on 24 June 1997. The Court quashed the judgment and confirmed the decision of 3 April 1996.

Parliament has taken the view that for the period during which they are in custody convicted prisoners have forfeited their right to have a say in the way the country is governed. The application was brought by the mother of a boy who suffered from learning difficulties. The headmaster and a teacher at the school he attended had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in a non-residential therapeutic school on 2 March 1992. The case was heard by the Swedish Court of Appeal, which ruled in favour of the mother. The judge found that the application had been brought by a woman who was not mentally ill and that her son should not have been placed in a therapeutic school. He ruled that the case should be dismissed on the grounds that the woman had no mental illness.

The applicant's son was placed in a non-residential therapeutic school in 1992. The headmaster and a teacher at the school had expressed concern about his learning difficulties and his general state of health. In October 1991 they had contacted the Social Council and expressed concern. Following this, the Council commenced an investigation which, with Mrs Andersson's agreement, led to the placement of her son in the therapeutic school. The case is still ongoing and will be heard by the European Court of Human Rights in Paris in April 2013. The judge will decide whether the case should go to the European court of human rights in Strasbourg, France, in May 2013.

The tribunal dismissed the applicant's complaints in. relation to his dismissal and the manner of his dismissal.
